name: AH-1 Cobra
tagline: The Bell AH-1 Cobra is a two-seat attack helicopter built by Bell for the U.S. Army and the first dedicated attack helicopter to enter large-scale service. It reached Vietnam in 1967, where Cobras flew more than a million operational hours.
quickFacts: The Cobra was developed from the UH-1 Huey and reused about 80 percent of its parts, including the engine, transmission and rotor system.
The prototype Model 209 rolled out on 3 September 1965 and first flew four days later, on 7 September.
Cobras flew more than one million operational hours in Vietnam, and about 300 of the nearly 1,110 delivered were lost to combat and accidents.
Operation Lam Son 719 in Laos destroyed 26 AH-1Gs and damaged 158.
Iraqi Mi-25s and Iranian AH-1J SeaCobras fought the only confirmed helicopter-versus-helicopter air battles during the Iran-Iraq War.
The crew sat in stepped tandem seats, with the gunner in the front seat for the best visibility and the commander behind.

specifications.specificationsNote: Specifications are for the original AH-1G. The Army's later AH-1F had a 1,800 shp T53-L-703 engine, an empty weight of 6,600 lb, a maximum takeoff weight of 10,000 lb, a range of 274 nmi and a service ceiling of 12,200 ft. Sources give the AH-1G's T53-L-13 as both 1,100 shp and 1,400 shp; the lower figure is used. The service entry date is the day the first six reached Bien Hoa. The retired date is the Marine Corps' 2020 withdrawal of the AH-1W, as the last major Cobra user; the Army retired the type from active service in March 1999 and from the reserves in September 2001.

variants.desc: The initial 1966 production version for the U.S. Army, with a T53-L-13 engine and an M28 chin turret. Bell built 1,116 from 1967 to 1973, and the Army's fleet peaked at 1,081 aircraft. The first six reached Bien Hoa, Vietnam, on 30 August 1967.

Army upgrades. The AH-1Q added TOW anti-tank missiles, and the AH-1S added the T53-L-703 engine. The modernised AH-1F had a 1,800 shp engine, a weight of 10,000 lb and a range of 274 nmi. Japan built 89 AH-1S under licence at Fuji from 1984 to 2000.
A twin-engine version ordered by the U.S. Marine Corps in 1968. The AH-1T was a later Marine upgrade with a longer fuselage and tailboom.
The Marine Corps' twin-engine version, retired from U.S. service in 2020. Turkey bought ten AH-1Ws alongside 32 ex-U.S. Army Cobras.
A later development for the U.S. Marine Corps. The sources list it as a related aircraft rather than as a Cobra variant, and it follows the AH-1W, which the Marines retired in 2020.

overview: The Bell AH-1 Cobra is a two-seat, single-rotor attack helicopter built by Bell Helicopter for the U.S. Army. It was the first dedicated attack helicopter to enter large-scale service, and the first AH-1Gs reached Vietnam in 1967. {{ref:wiki-ah1}} {{ref:maps}}

Bell built 1,116 AH-1Gs for the Army between 1967 and 1973, and Cobras logged more than a million operational hours in Vietnam. The type was developed into twin-engine versions for the U.S. Marine Corps and exported to Japan, Israel, Turkey and others. {{ref:wiki-ah1}} {{ref:maps}}

sections.heading: Origins & Concept
paragraphs: The Cobra grew out of the UH-1 Iroquois as the Bell Model 209, which used the Huey's engine, transmission and rotor system with a new, narrow fuselage. About 80 percent of its components already had Huey part numbers. The prototype rolled out on 3 September 1965 and first flew four days later. {{ref:wiki-ah1}}

The Army applied the Cobra name to the AH-1G designation, after Bell added Cobra to the Huey nickname to make HueyCobra. The aircraft was first designated UH-1H, and the A for attack was soon adopted. {{ref:wiki-ah1}}

sections.heading: Design & Engineering
paragraphs: The AH-1G has stepped tandem seating, with the gunner in the forward seat for the best visibility and the commander behind him. Both seats have flight controls and armoured seats. A chin-mounted M28 turret carries two 7.62 mm miniguns, two M129 40 mm grenade launchers, or one of each. {{ref:wiki-ah1}}

The stub wings carry 2.75 in rockets in 7-tube M158 or 19-tube M200 launchers. The AH-1G was 53 ft (16.2 m) long with its rotors turning, weighed 9,500 lb at takeoff and used a Lycoming T53-L-13 turboshaft for a top speed of 149 kn. {{ref:wiki-ah1}} {{ref:maps}}

sections.heading: Vietnam & Combat History
paragraphs: The first six AH-1Gs arrived at Bien Hoa on 30 August 1967, and the 334th Assault Helicopter Company became operational on 6 October 1967. The first combat kill was a sampan on 4 September 1967. Cobras flew fire support, escorted transports and worked in hunter-killer teams with OH-6A scouts, and the Army flew the type in Vietnam until the withdrawal in 1973. {{ref:wiki-ah1}}

About 300 of the nearly 1,110 Cobras delivered were lost to combat and accidents. Operation Lam Son 719 in Laos destroyed 26 AH-1Gs and damaged 158. In the Iran-Iraq War, Iraqi Mi-25s and Iranian AH-1J SeaCobras fought the only confirmed air-to-air battles between helicopters, with 10 SeaCobras and 6 Mi-25s destroyed. {{ref:wiki-ah1}} {{ref:maps}} {{ref:wiki-mi24}}

sections.heading: Marine Cobras & Exports
paragraphs: The Marine Corps ordered the twin-engine AH-1J in 1968, followed by the longer AH-1T and the AH-1W SuperCobra, which the Marines retired in 2020. Two of four AH-1Ts involved in the 1983 Grenada invasion were lost to anti-aircraft fire on the first day. {{ref:wiki-ah1}}

Israel bought six AH-1Gs, formed its first attack helicopter squadron on 1 December 1977 and made its first attack on 9 May 1979 near Tyre, Lebanon. Japan built 89 AH-1S under licence from 1984 to 2000, and Turkey operated ten AH-1Ws and 32 ex-U.S. Army Cobras. The Army removed the type from the reserves in September 2001, but the U.S. Forest Service converted 25 AH-1Fs into Firewatch Cobras, the last two of which retired in October 2021. {{ref:wiki-ah1}}

survivors.intro: Cobras are preserved in museums across the United States; the airframes below are individually documented.

airframes.name: AH-1S Cobra
airframes.note: Donated on 13 May 1996 with 2,008 flight hours. It served with units at Fort Hood, deployed to Germany with NATO from 1976 to 1978, and later flew with the Ohio Air National Guard.

airframes.name: Bell 209 demonstrator
airframes.note: The original demonstrator, retired to the museum.
